Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 32, verse 4:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days; then He established Himself above the Throne. You have, apart from Him, no protector and no intercessor. Will you not then remember?﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: The Deity whom none is worthy of worship except Him, O people, ﴿created the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ of creation, ﴿in six days﴾, then ﴿established Himself above His Throne﴾ on the seventh day, after His creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them.

As related from:

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿He created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days; then He established Himself above the Throne﴾: on the seventh day. He says: You have no god, O people, other than the One who did this deed and created this wondrous creation in six days.

* * *

And His words: ﴿You have, apart from Him, no protector and no intercessor﴾

He says: You have, O people, apart from Him, no protector who takes charge of your affairs and gives you victory against Him if He wills harm for you, nor an intercessor who intercedes for you with Him if He punishes you for your disobedience to Him. He says: So take Him alone as your protector, and seek help in your affairs through Him and through obedience to Him, for He will protect you when He wills to protect you from whoever intends you evil, and no one can repel from you what He Himself wills for you, because no subduer can overpower Him and no conqueror can overcome Him. ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Will you not then take heed and reflect, O people, so that you know that you have no protector or intercessor apart from Him, and thus single Him out for divinity and devote worship sincerely to Him, and renounce what is beside Him of rivals and deities?

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 32, verse 5:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him in a Day, the extent of which is a thousand years of what you count﴾ (5).

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: Allah is the One who arranges the affair concerning His creation from the heaven to the earth, then it ascends to Him.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed regarding the meaning of His saying: ﴿then it ascends to Him in a Day, the extent of which is a thousand years of what you count﴾. Some of them said: its meaning is that the command descends from the heaven to the earth and ascends from the earth to the heaven in one day, and the measure of that is a thousand years of the days of this world that you count; because the distance between the earth and the heaven is five hundred years, and the distance between the heaven and the earth is like that, so that is a thousand years.

Mention of those who said that:

- Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Hakkam related to us, from 'Amr ibn Ma'ruf, from Layth, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿in a day the extent of which is a thousand years﴾: he means by that the descent of the command from the heaven to the earth, and its ascent from the earth to the heaven, in one day, and that is its measure of a thousand years; because the distance between the heaven and the earth is a journey of five hundred years.

- Bishr related to us, he said: Yazid related to us, he said: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth, then it ascends to Him in a day﴾ of your days ﴿the extent of which is a thousand years of what you count﴾: he says: the extent of its journey in that day is a thousand years of what you count of your days, of the days of this world: five hundred years for its descent and five hundred years for its ascent, so that is a thousand years.

- Ibn Waki' related to us, he said: Abu Mu'awiyah related to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, regarding ﴿then it ascends to Him in a day the extent of which is a thousand years of what you count﴾, he said: the angels ascend to the heaven, then descend, in a day of your days, and that is a journey of a thousand years.

- He said: my father related to us, from Sufyan, from Simak, from Ikrimah, regarding ﴿a thousand years of what you count﴾, he said: of the days of this world.

- Hannad ibn al-Sarri related to us, he said: Abu al-Ahwas related to us, from Abu al-Harith, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth, then it ascends to Him in a day﴾ of your days, the journey between the heaven and the earth is five hundred years.

It is related from 'Abd al-Razzaq, he said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, who said: the matters descend and ascend from the heaven to the earth in one day, its measure being a thousand years: five hundred until it descends, and five hundred until it ascends.

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth, then it ascends to Him in one of the six days in which Allah created the creation; the measure of that day was a thousand years of what you count of your days.

Mention of those who said that:

- Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Hakkam related to us, from 'Anbasah, from Simak, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿a thousand years of what you count﴾, he said: that is the measure of the journey. His saying: ﴿like a thousand years of what you count﴾, he said: Allah created the heavens and the earth in six days, and each of these days is like a thousand years of what you count.

- Ibn Waki' related to us, he said: my father related to us, from Isra'il, from Simak, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿in a day the extent of which is a thousand years of what you count﴾, he said: the six days in which Allah created the heavens and the earth.

- It was related to me from al-Husayn, he said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd informed us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His saying: ﴿in a day the extent of which is a thousand years of what you count﴾: he means this day, from the six days in which Allah created the heavens and the earth and what is between them.

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth through the angels, then the angels ascend to Him, in a day the extent of which is a thousand years of the days of this world.

Mention of those who said that:

- Ali related to me, he said: 'Abd Allah related to us, he said: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿then it ascends to Him in a day the extent of which is a thousand years﴾, he said: this is in the world; the angels ascend to Him in a day the extent of which is a thousand years.

- Ibn Waki' related to us, he said: Ghundar related to us, from Shu'bah, from Simak, from Ikrimah: ﴿in a day the extent of which is a thousand years﴾, he said: what is between the heaven and the earth is a journey of a thousand years of what you count of the days of the Hereafter. [[In al-Durr al-Manthur: "of the days of this world"; and it is clear. End.]]

- Ibn al-Muthanna related to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far related to us, he said: Shu'bah related to us, from Simak, from Ikrimah, that he said regarding this verse: ﴿it ascends to Him in a day the extent of which is a thousand years of what you count﴾, he said: what is between the heaven and the earth is a journey of a thousand years.

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth, in a day the measure of that arrangement is a thousand years of the days of this world; then that arrangement ascends to Him, the arrangement which He arranged.

Mention of those who said that:

It is related from Hajjaj, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, that he said: He decides the matter of each thing for a thousand years to the angels, then so on until a thousand years pass; then He decides the matter of each thing for a thousand years, and so on forever. He said: ﴿a day, the extent of which﴾: the day is what is said to what He decides for the angels for a thousand years: "Be," and it is. But He named it a day, He named it as we have explained. All of that is from Mujahid. He said: and His saying: ﴿and indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ (22:47): he said: it is the same.

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth, then it ascends to Allah in a day the extent of which is a thousand years, the measure of the ascent is a thousand years of what you count.

Mention of those who said that:

- Yunus related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: ﴿then it ascends to Him in a day the extent of which is a thousand years of what you count﴾: some people of knowledge said: the measure between the earth, when it ascends to Him, until it reaches its ascent, is a thousand years; this is the measure of that ascent in that day in which it ascends.

The most correct of these sayings in my view is the saying of the one who said: its meaning is: He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth, then it ascends to Him in a day, the measure of that day in the ascent of that matter to Him and its descent to the earth being a thousand years of what you count of your days: five hundred in the descent and five hundred in the ascent; because that is the most evident of its meanings and the most fitting to the apparent sense of the revelation.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 32, verses 6–8:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿That is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Mighty, the Merciful (6) who perfected everything He created, and began the creation of man from clay (7) then made his offspring from an extract of a liquid, despised (8)﴾

He, may He be exalted, says: This One who does what I have described to you in these verses is ﴿the Knower of the unseen﴾, meaning the Knower of what is hidden from your sight, O people, so you do not perceive it, of what hearts conceal and souls hide, and of what has not yet come into being but will be. ﴿And the witnessed﴾ means what eyes have witnessed, so they have seen it and observed it, and what exists. ﴿The Mighty﴾ means: severe in punishing those who disbelieve in Him, associate others with Him, and deny His messengers. ﴿The Merciful﴾ means: toward those who repent from their error, return to belief in Him and His messenger, and act in obedience to Him, by not punishing them after repentance.

* *

As for His words: ﴿who perfected everything He created﴾

The reciters differed in reading this. Some reciters of Makkah, Madinah and Basra read ﴿aḥsana kulla shay'in khalqahu﴾ with a sukun on the lam (khalqahu). Some Madinans and most Kufans read ﴿aḥsana kulla shay'in khalaqahu﴾ with a fatha on the lam.

The correct view on this, in my opinion, is that both are well-known readings, each recited by reputable reciters, and both are sound in meaning. This is because God perfected His creation, and perfected everything He created. So whichever of the two a reader recites, he is correct.

The interpreters differed on its meaning. Some of them said: its meaning is: He perfected everything and made it firm.

Those who said so:

* Al-'Abbas ibn Abi Talib narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn ibn Ibrahim Ishkab [[In al-Taj (shkb): Ishkab, the epithet of al-Husayn ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Hasan ibn Za'lan al-'Amiri, the teacher of Abu Bakr ibn Abi al-Dunya.]] narrated to us, saying: Sharik narrated to us, from Khasif, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿who perfected everything He created﴾, he said: Indeed, the rump of the monkey is not beautiful, but He made its form firm.

* Ibn Wakī' narrated to me, saying: Abu al-Nadr narrated to us, saying: Abu Sa'id al-Mu'addib narrated to us, from Khasif, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he used to read it: ﴿who perfected everything He created﴾, and he said: Indeed, the rump of the monkey is not beautiful, but He made it firm.

* Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, ﴿aḥsana kulla shay'in khalqahu﴾, he said: He perfected everything He created.

* Muhammad ibn 'Ammarah narrated to me, saying: 'Abdullah ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: Isra'il narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, ﴿aḥsana kulla shay'in﴾: he counted everything.

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: He who made the creation of everything good.

Those who said so:

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿who perfected everything He created﴾: He made it good in the manner in which He created it.

It is mentioned from al-Hajjaj, from Ibn Jurayj, from al-A'raj, from Mujahid, that he said: it is like ﴿who gave everything its creation, then guided [it]﴾. He said: He did not make the creation of animals within the creation of humans, nor the creation of humans within the creation of animals, but He created everything and measured it with precise measure.

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: He knew everything He created, as if they directed the interpretation of the statement toward the meaning that He inspired His creation with what they need, and that His words ﴿aḥsana﴾ are from the saying of a speaker: so-and-so does such-and-such well (yuḥsinu), when he knows it.

Those who said so:

* Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to us, from Sharik, from Khasif, from Mujahid, ﴿aḥsana kulla shay'in khalqahu﴾, he said: He gave everything its creation: man to man, the horse to the horse, and the donkey to the donkey. On this view, "khalq" and "kull" are in the accusative by the governing of "aḥsana" over them.

The most correct of the sayings on this, in my view, according to the reading of the one who reads ﴿alladhīna aḥsana kulla shay'in khalqahu﴾ with a fatha on the lam, is the saying of the one who said: its meaning is He made firm and perfected. This is because there is no meaning to it when recited this way except one of two: either this meaning of firmness and perfection which we have stated, or the meaning of making good, which is in the sense of beauty and goodness. Since in His creation there is what no one doubts is ugly and repulsive, it is known that He did not intend that He made beautiful everything He created, but that He made it firm and perfected its craftsmanship. As for the other reading, which has a sukun on the lam, the most correct interpretation of it is the saying of the one who said: its meaning is: He knew and inspired everything He created, He is the best of them, as He said: ﴿who gave everything its creation, then guided [it]﴾, because that is the clearest of its meanings. As for the one who directed the interpretation of it to mean: who made the creation of everything good, he made "khalq" an accusative of specification, as if he said: who made every thing good in creation. Some of them said: it is of the preposed which means the postposed, and they direct it to being like the saying of the poet:

"And my journey toward you at night, when it hugs me [in darkness], / is for that [night] when the fool-coward takes fright" [[The verse is in Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubaydah (p. 192a), explaining the verse "who perfected everything He created," where he said: its metaphor is: "aḥsana khalqa kulli shay'in"; the Arabs do this, placing first and last. He said: "my journey toward you..." the verse means: my journey when the night embraced me toward you. In Lisan (ḥḍn): "ḥaḍanā al-mafāza" means its two sides; "ḥaḍanā al-layl" means its two sides; "ḥaḍan al-jabal" is what one can endure; "ḥaḍanā al-shay'" are its two sides. Al-Hadan, on the pattern of kitab, is the stupid, coarse, sluggish, heavy one in war. In the hadith of 'Uthman: "a coward, a hadan."]]

meaning: "my journey, the night's embrace of me, toward you"; and like the saying of another:

"As if Hind's front teeth and her radiance / on the day we met at the burrows of Dabbab" [[The verse is in Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubaydah (p. 192a), at the interpretation of "aḥsana kulla shay'in khalqahu," after the previous witness: "my journey toward you..." Then he said: "as if Hind's front teeth and radiance." It is also in Lisan (dbb): He said: Al-Azhari said: in al-Khalsa there is sand called al-Dabbab, and opposite it are many dahlan (with a damma on the dal), and from it is the saying of the poet: "As if Hind's front teeth and her radiance, when we met near the burrows of Dabbab..." Also: "Turned away, with noses, the spring rain has given them / over bright patches, having gone toward plants." Al-adhal and al-dahlan are plurals of dahl, with a fatha, which is a narrow-mouthed hole that widens at its bottom until one can walk into it.]]

that is: as if Hind's front teeth and her radiance.

* * *

As for His words: ﴿and began the creation of man from clay﴾

He, may He be exalted, says: and He began the creation of Adam from clay. ﴿Then He made his offspring﴾ means: his descendants, ﴿from an extract﴾, he says: from the water that was extracted and emerged from him. It only means from a discharge of his water, as the poet said:

"So she brought him forth, a sharp-edged, lion-like one, / an extract of a womb that was not secure" [[The verse is in Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubaydah (p. 162b), at His words, "And We certainly created man from an extract of clay," in Surah al-Mu'minun (vol. 18: 8). Refer to it there.]]

* * *

As for His words: ﴿from a despised liquid﴾

He says: from a weak, thin drop.

The interpreters said what is similar to what we have said in interpreting this.

Those who said so:

You were a speck of dust in a turbid, foaming wave,
which the flood carried and in which you went astray, a going astray.

[The verse is by al-Akhṭal (his Dīwān, Beirut edition, p. 50). Qadhā is what falls into the eye of dust, straw or the like, which the wind carries. Akdar is turbid, not clear, because it came from afar; it runs strongly, mixed with dust and debris, and for this reason he said "foaming", which is that over which foam has risen because of its agitation and turbulence. Atī is the torrent that comes from a distant place, or from one land to another. Before this verse is another verse connected to it in meaning, in which al-Akhṭal said: "And when he calls them to glory, the two branches of Wāʾil, and the valley gathers against you and flows." The two branches of Wāʾil are Bakr and Taghlib. He means that when the two branches of Wāʾil gather in one place on a day of boasting with the tribes, and become like a flood in their abundance, you, O Jarīr, in comparison with them were nothing but a speck that drowned in that turbid flood, went astray in it and disappeared, and no trace of it could be found. For this reason the commentator of the Dīwān said: the meaning of the verse is that Jarīr's father is base and contemptible compared with those mentioned. The verse is evidence that ḍalāl means the disappearance of a thing, so that no trace of it can be perceived.]

[The verse is by al-Akhṭal (his Dīwān, Beirut edition, p. 50). Qadhā is what falls into the eye of dust, straw or the like, which the wind carries. Akdar is turbid, not clear, because it came from afar; it runs strongly, mixed with dust and debris, and for this reason he said "foaming", which is that over which foam has risen because of its agitation and turbulence. Atī is the torrent that comes from a distant place, or from one land to another. Before this verse is another verse connected to it in meaning, in which al-Akhṭal said: "And when he calls them to glory, the two branches of Wāʾil, and the valley gathers against you and flows." The two branches of Wāʾil are Bakr and Taghlib. He means that when the two branches of Wāʾil gather in one place on a day of boasting with the tribes, and become like a flood in their abundance, you, O Jarīr, in comparison with them were nothing but a speck that drowned in that turbid flood, went astray in it and disappeared, and no trace of it could be found. For this reason the commentator of the Dīwān said: the meaning of the verse is that Jarīr's father is base and contemptible compared with those mentioned. The verse is evidence that ḍalāl means the disappearance of a thing, so that no trace of it can be perceived.]

**The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds; they call upon their Lord in fear and hope, and they spend of what We have provided them﴾ (16)**

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: The sides of these people who believe in the signs of God, whose description I have given, withdraw and rise from the beds on which they lie down to sleep, and they do not sleep. ﴿They call upon their Lord in fear and hope﴾ for His pardon toward them and His favour upon them through His mercy and forgiveness. ﴿And of what We have provided them, they spend﴾ in the way of God, and they discharge from it the rights of God which He has made obligatory upon them in it.

*Tatajafa* (تتجافى) means to withdraw, from *al-jafa'*, and *al-jafa'* means to rise away (*al-nabw*), as the rajaz poet said:

"My companion is a swift she-camel of Dimashq (*hibab*), / and the son of Mulat, the one who stands apart and is most gentle (*arfaq*)."[[The two lines are by al-Zaffan (see them in the appendix to the Diwan of al-'Ajjaj, 100). *Al-hibab* means vigour and haste in travel. *Al-Dimashq* is a light, swift she-camel. Abu 'Ubayda cited al-Zaffan's line: "A watering place full of the *al-Ghalfaq* plant, / it shines or the *al-Khawarnaq* spreads over it. / I came to it while the night was dark and dappled, / and my companion was a swift she-camel of Dimashq, / like a boat after weariness." The author did not mention the second line, which is the point of evidence for him. In *Lisan al-'Arab* (root *mlt*), al-Nadr said: *al-Mula<u>t</u>an* are what is on the right and left of the camel's saddle-girth (*al-kurkara*). The "two sons of Mulat" of a camel are the two upper arms, and it is said they are its shoulders; "sons of Mulat" are the upper arms and shoulders, singular "son of Mulat". Ibn al-Sikkit said: the "sons of Mulat" are the upper arms. *Al-Mutajafi* is the one separated from its side, and that is stronger for its travel. *Al-Arfaq* is the one whose elbow is turned away from its side; it is "more gentle", and a gentle she-camel is *raf'a'*. End of quotation. Al-Azhari said: what he memorised with this meaning is "*naqah daf'a'*" and "*jamal adfaq*", when its elbow has splayed from its side. In *Lisan al-'Arab* (root *dfq*): a man is *adfaq* when his back is bent from age or grief. Al-Mufaddal recited: "*And the son of Mulat, withdrawing, most bent.*" End of quotation. Abu 'Ubayda cited the two lines in *Majaz al-Qur'an* (folio 193a) without attributing them. Then he said: *adfaq* (with *dal*) means withdrawn from its *kurkara*. End of quotation.]]

The meaning is that the she-camel's side separates from the son of Mulat. God, may His remembrance be exalted, described them by the withdrawal of their sides from their beds because they abandon lying down to sleep, occupied with prayer.

- It was related to me from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say concerning His words: ﴿their sides forsake their beds; they call upon their Lord in fear and hope﴾: "They are a people who never cease to remember God, whether in prayer, or standing, or sitting, or when they awake from their sleep. Whenever they awake, they remember God, whether in prayer, or standing, or sitting, or lying on their sides. They never cease to remember God."

The correct view on this matter is to say that God described these people as having their sides rising from their beds, occupied with calling upon their Lord and worshipping Him in fear and hope. This withdrawal of their sides from their beds happens at night, because what is known from the describer's description of a man whose side has risen from his bed is that he has withdrawn from sleep at the time when people normally sleep, and that time is the night, not the day. The Arabs likewise describe a man in this way when they describe him so. This is shown by the words of 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha al-Ansari, may God be pleased with him, describing the Prophet of God ﷺ:

"He spends the night, his side withdrawn from his bed, / when the beds grow heavy with the polytheists."[[This line is by 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha al-Ansari, one of the poets of the Prophet ﷺ. *Yujafi* means he keeps away; *istathqalat* means became heavy; *al-madaji'* is the plural of *madja'*, the bedding on which one sleeps or its place. The line is a second piece of evidence for *tatajafa* in God's words: "their sides forsake their beds", meaning: they keep away. Abu 'Ubayda said in *Majaz al-Qur'an* (folio 195b): that is, they rise from it and withdraw, because they pray at night. End of quotation.]]

Since this is so, and since God, may His remembrance be exalted, did not restrict His description of these people, with their sides withdrawn from their beds, to a particular state or time of the night rather than another, it is necessary that this should be true at every hour and time of the night. If so, then whoever prays between Maghrib and 'Isha', or waits for the *'Isha'* prayer, or stands in prayer at night or part of it, or remembers God during the hours of the night, or prays the *'atamah*, is included in the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿their sides forsake their beds﴾, because his side has withdrawn from his bed in the state in which he stands for prayer, whether he prays standing or remembers God, or sits, provided he is not lying down, and he is able to stand or sit. Nevertheless, although this is so, directing the speech to the meaning of standing in prayer at night is more pleasing to me, because that is the most evident of its meanings, the most prevalent in the apparent sense of the speech, and a report from the Messenger of God ﷺ has come to this effect.

**The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words, exalted is He:** ﴿So no soul knows what has been hidden for them of the delight of the eyes, as a reward for what they used to do (32:17)﴾

God, remembered is He, says: No soul of any living being knows what God has hidden for those whose description, exalted is His praise, He gave in these two verses, of what gladdens their eyes in His gardens on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾, meaning: as a recompense for them for their deeds which they used to do in the world.

Those who engage in interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said the same as what we have said about this.

Qur'an reciters differed regarding the recitation of His words: ﴿So no soul knows what has been hidden for them of the delight of the eyes﴾. Some of the Medinese and Basrans, and some of the Kufans, read it: ﴿ukhfiya (has been hidden)﴾ with a damma on the alif and a fatha on the ya', in the sense of the passive form fu'ila (it has been done). Some of the Kufans read: ﴿ukhfi lahum (I have hidden for them)﴾ with a damma on the alif and the ya' left unvowelled, in the sense of af'ala (the first person): "I have hidden for them."

The correct view on this, in our opinion, is that both are well-known readings, close in meaning, because when God hides it, it is hidden, and when it is hidden, it has no concealer other than Him. And the "ma" in His words: ﴿So no soul knows what has been hidden for them﴾, when it is taken to mean "that which" (alladhi), it is in the accusative case through the verb "knows" falling upon it, however the reader reads "ukhfiya." And when it is directed to the meaning of "ayyu" (which), it is in the nominative case when "ukhfa" is read with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the alif, since the subject is not named; and when "ukhfi" is read with the ya' left unvowelled, it is in the accusative case through the verb "ukhfi" falling upon it.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 32, verses 18–20:

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was defiantly disobedient? They are not equal.﴾ (18) ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will have the Gardens of Refuge as lodging, in recompense for what they used to do.﴾ (19) ﴿But as for those who defied, their refuge is the Fire. Every time they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it, and it will be said to them, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾ (20)

He, the Exalted, says: Is this disbelieving one, who denies the promise and threat of God and opposes the command and prohibition of God, like this believer in God, who affirms His promise and threat and obeys Him in His command and prohibition? No, they are not equal before God, meaning: the disbelievers in God and the believers in Him are not equal in His sight regarding what He will do with them on the Day of Resurrection. He said ﴿they are not equal﴾ in the plural, whereas He had earlier mentioned two: "a believer" and "a defiantly disobedient one," because He did not intend by "the believer" a single believer, nor by "the defiantly disobedient" a single sinner; rather He intended all the sinners and all the believers in God. When two are not specifically intended, the Arabs treat them in the manner of the plural.

It has been mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with him, and al-Walid ibn ʿUqbah.

Mention of those who said this:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, he said: Ibn Ishaq related to me, from some of his companions, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār, who said: It was revealed in Medina concerning ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and al-Walid ibn ʿUqbah ibn Abī Muʿayṭ. There was some speech between al-Walid and ʿAlī. Al-Walid ibn ʿUqbah said: "I am more eloquent of tongue than you, sharper of spear than you, and more firm in the ranks of the army than you." ʿAlī said: "Be silent, for you are a defiant sinner." So God revealed concerning the two of them: ﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was defiantly disobedient? They are not equal.﴾ up to His saying: ﴿that you used to deny.﴾

Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was defiantly disobedient? They are not equal.﴾ He said: "No, by God, they are not equal in this world, nor at death, nor in the Hereafter."

* *

As for His saying: ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will have the Gardens of Refuge﴾

He, the Exalted, says: As for those who affirmed God and His Messenger and acted upon what God and His Messenger commanded them, they will have the Gardens of Refuge: meaning the gardens of the dwellings in which they will reside in the Hereafter and to which they will repair.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿as lodging, in recompense for what they used to do﴾

He says: as a lodging which He has granted them as a reward from Him for what they used to do in this world by obeying Him.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿But as for those who defied﴾

He, the Exalted, says: As for those who disbelieved in God and departed from His obedience, ﴿their refuge is the Fire﴾, meaning: their dwellings to which they will repair in the Hereafter are the Fire. ﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it, and it will be said to them, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to﴾ in this world ﴿deny﴾ that God prepared it for the people who associate others with Him."

The people of interpretation have said something similar to what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said this:

Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿But as for those who defied﴾: they associated partners (with God). ﴿And it will be said to them, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾ And the people were deniers, as you see.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 32, verse 22:

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the verses of his Lord, then turns away from them? Indeed, We will take retribution upon the criminals.﴾

His saying, may He be remembered: And which of the people is more unjust to himself than the one whom Allah has admonished with His proofs, His verses of Scripture, and His messengers, and then he turns away from all of that, so he does not heed its admonitions, but rather becomes arrogant toward them.

* *

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will take retribution upon the criminals.﴾

He says: Indeed, We will take retribution upon those who earned sins and committed evil deeds.

His, the Exalted's, statement means: they guide their followers and those among them who accept, by Our permission to them to do so and Our strengthening them in it.

* *

And His statement: ﴿when they were patient﴾

The readers differed in the recitation of this. The majority of the readers of Medina and Basra, and some of the people of Kufa, recited ﴿lamma ṣabaru﴾ with a fatha on the lam and a shadda on the mim, meaning: "idh ṣabaru" (when they were patient) and "ḥīna ṣabaru" (at the time they were patient). The meaning of the speech when it is recited with a fatha on the lam and a shadda on the mim is: We made from among them leaders who guide their followers by Our permission to them and Our strengthening them in guidance, since they were patient in obeying Us and restrained themselves from the pleasures and desires of the world. And when it is recited with a kasra on the lam [[probably "fa-yakūnu 'alā..." etc.]] according to what we have described.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 32, verse 27:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have they not seen that We drive the water to the barren land, and bring forth thereby crops of which their cattle and they themselves eat? Will they not then see?﴾

Exalted is He, says: Have these deniers of the Resurrection after death, and of being raised after annihilation, not seen that by Our power We drive water to the dry, hard land which has no vegetation? The root of this is from their saying: a she-camel is jarz (jurooz) when she eats everything, and likewise the land is jurooz (juruz) when nothing remains on its surface but that it destroys it, like the camel's eating of everything she finds. From this they say of a man who eats much: jarooz, as the rajiz (poet) said:

Khabb jaroozun wa idha... [[This is part of a line of mashtur rajaz verse, cited by al-Shawkani in his tafsir titled Fath al-Qadir (4: 249), edition of Mustafa al-Babi al-Halabi and his sons. The complete line with what follows there is: "Khabb jaroozun wa idha jaa'a bakaa ... wa ya'kulu al-tamra wa la yulqi al-nawa" (a glutton and a crier when hungry, who eats dates and does not spit out the pits).

It is evidence in the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: (Have they not seen that We drive the water to the barren land). Abu 'Ubayda said in Majaz al-Qur'an (folio 193a): al-ardh al-juruz: i.e., the dry, hard land that has not been touched by rain. End quote. And al-Farra' said in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (folio 253): al-jurz is that in which there is no vegetation. It is said of a she-camel: innaha la-jarrazun, when she eats everything, and of a man: innahu la-jarooz, when he is a great eater. And a sword is sayf jarrazun when it leaves nothing without cutting it.]]

From this, the sword that leaves nothing without cutting is called sayf jarrāz. It has four dialectal forms: ardh juruz, jarz, jirz, and juz; and the fatha form is attributed to Banu Tamim, as I have been informed.

Those who engaged in interpretation have said things similar to what we have said on this matter.

﴿and bring forth thereby crops of which their cattle and they themselves eat﴾: Exalted is He, says: We bring forth by that water which We drive to it, despite its dryness, hardness and long time without water, green crops, of which their livestock eat and by which their bodies and frames are nourished, so that they live by it. ﴿Will they not then see?﴾: Exalted is He, says: Will they not see that with their own eyes, so that by seeing it they know that the power by which We did that is not beyond Me to bring the dead back to life, raise them from their graves, and return them in the forms they had before their death?

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 32, verse 28–30:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿And they say, "When is this victory, if you should be truthful?"﴾ [32:28] ﴿Say, "On the Day of Victory, the faith of those who disbelieved will not benefit them, nor will they be reprieved."﴾ [32:29] ﴿So turn away from them and wait; indeed, they are [also] waiting.﴾ [32:30]

His, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And they say﴾ — these polytheists, O Muhammad, to you: ﴿"When is this victory?"﴾ There has been difference of opinion regarding the meaning of this. Some of them said: its meaning is, "When will this judgment between us and you come, and when will this reward and punishment occur?"

Mention of those who said this:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿And they say, "When is this victory, if you should be truthful?"﴾ He said: The companions of the Prophet of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, for us there is a day which is near, on which we will rest and be blessed." So the polytheists said: ﴿"When is this victory, if you should be truthful?"﴾

Others said: Rather, it refers to the conquest of Makkah.

The correct view on this matter is the view of the one who said: its meaning is, "And they say: When will this judgment between us and you come," meaning the punishment. What indicates that this is its meaning is His words: ﴿Say, "On the Day of Victory, the faith of those who disbelieved will not benefit them, nor will they be reprieved."﴾ There is no doubt that Allah had made repentance available to the disbelievers before the conquest of Makkah and after it. And if the meaning of His words ﴿"When is this victory?"﴾ were as the one who said it refers to the conquest of Makkah stated, then there would be no repentance for those among the polytheists who embraced Islam after the conquest of Makkah. And there is no doubt that Allah accepted the repentance of many of the polytheists after the conquest of Makkah, and benefited them by their faith in Him and His Messenger. Thus it is known from this the soundness of what we have said in interpretation and the corruption of what contradicts it.

* *

His words: ﴿If you should be truthful﴾

That is: if you are truthful in what you say, that we will be punished for our denial of Muhammad ﷺ and our worship of the deities and idols.

* *

His words: ﴿Say, "On the Day of Victory"﴾

He says to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: Say, O Muhammad, to them: On the day of judgment and the coming of the punishment, the faith that they produce at that time will not benefit those who disbelieved in Allah and His signs.

As narrated:

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: ﴿Say, "On the Day of Victory, the faith of those who disbelieved will not benefit them"﴾ — he said: "The Day of Victory is when the punishment comes."

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿Yawm al-Fath﴾ — "the Day of Victory" — is the Day of Resurrection. The word "day" in His words ﴿Say, "On the Day of Victory"﴾ is in the accusative as a response to "when" (matā), because "when" is in the accusative position. The meaning of the speech is: "When is the time of this victory, if you are truthful?" Then it was said: "A day such-and-such," and the reciters recited it thus.

* *

His words: ﴿Nor will they be reprieved﴾

He says: nor will they be delayed for repentance and returning.

* *

His words: ﴿So turn away from them and wait; indeed, they are [also] waiting﴾

He says to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: So turn away, O Muhammad, from these polytheists who say to you, "When is this victory," seeking to hasten the punishment upon you, and wait to see what Allah will do with them; indeed, they are waiting for what you threaten them with of punishment and the coming of the Hour.

As narrated:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: ﴿So turn away from them and wait; indeed, they are [also] waiting﴾ — meaning the Day of Resurrection.

End of the commentary on Surah As-Sajdah, and to Allah belongs all praise and grace.
